q: When did Oscar Niemeyer receive the Pritzker Prize?
n: Oscar Niemeyer received the Pritzker Prize in 1988, shared with Gordon Bunshaft of SOM. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (1988 laureates).

q: Who designed the Bank of China Tower, the Louvre Pyramid and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame?
n: I.M. Pei designed the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong (1990), the Louvre Pyramid in Paris (1989) and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in Cleveland (1995). Source: Pei Cobb Freed & Partners; Pritzker Prize.

q: What is dominant in the work of I.M. Pei?
n: Pei's best-known works are built from pure geometric forms: the triangles and pyramids of the Louvre, the triangulated Bank of China Tower and the trapezoid-and-triangle East Building of the National Gallery. Geometric form is the broader dominant trait. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, I.M. Pei; Pritzker Prize jury citation (1983).

q: Which shape dominates the Bank of China Tower and the Louvre Pyramid?
n: The Louvre Pyramid and the Bank of China Tower are both built on triangles. The tower's facade is a lattice of triangulated braced frames, and the pyramid is triangular faces of glass. Source: Pei Cobb Freed & Partners; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Why did I.M. Pei choose a glass pyramid for the Louvre entrance?
o: To keep views of the historic palace while modernizing access
n: Pei chose transparent glass so the new main entrance would not hide or compete with the historic Louvre Palace around the Cour Napoléon, while the pyramid lit and organized the underground lobby. Source: Louvre official site (The Pyramid); Pei Cobb Freed & Partners.

q: What principle did Pei apply to the Louvre Pyramid?
o: Symmetry and axial alignment with the Cour Napoléon
n: The Louvre Pyramid is placed symmetrically on the historic axis that runs from the Louvre through the Tuileries to the Arc de Triomphe, centred in the Cour Napoléon. Source: Louvre official site; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Louvre Museum.

q: Who pioneered the use of béton brut (raw concrete)?
n: Auguste Perret pioneered exposed reinforced concrete as a finished architectural material, as at 25 bis rue Franklin (1903) and Le Raincy church (1923). Le Corbusier, who trained under him, later made béton brut a style. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Auguste Perret; UNESCO (Le Havre, rebuilt by Perret).

q: When was Fuller's Montreal geodesic dome built?
n: Buckminster Fuller's geodesic dome was the US Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal (1967), now the Biosphère. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Buckminster Fuller; Espace pour la vie Montréal (Biosphère).

q: Which architect loved curved lines and was a key figure of modern architecture?
n: Oscar Niemeyer favoured free, sensual curves over the right angle, as at Brasília and Pampulha. He wrote that he was drawn to the curves of Brazil's mountains and rivers. Source: Pritzker Architecture Prize (1988); Niemeyer, The Curves of Time.

q: What is Alvar Aalto's full name?
n: Alvar Aalto's full name was Hugo Alvar Henrik Aalto (1898–1976), the Finnish modernist known for humane, organic modernism. Source: Alvar Aalto Foundation; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: Which deconstructivist building by Frank Gehry is in Bilbao?
n: Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1997) is a landmark of deconstructivism, with curving forms designed with CATIA software. Source: Guggenheim Bilbao official site; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What clads the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao?
n: The curved forms of the Guggenheim Bilbao are clad in about 33,000 thin titanium panels, along with limestone and glass. Source: Guggenheim Bilbao official site (The Building).

q: Which is a work of Louis Sullivan?
n: The Wainwright Building in St. Louis (1891), by Adler & Sullivan, is an early steel-frame skyscraper expressing its height through vertical piers. Woolworth is by Cass Gilbert, Monadnock by Burnham & Root and Chrysler by William Van Alen. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Louis Sullivan; National Park Service (NHL).

q: The Greeks introduced proportion. Which architect reintroduced a proportion system in modern times?
n: Le Corbusier's Modulor (1948) is a proportion system based on human dimensions and the golden ratio, reviving classical proportional theory for modern design. Source: Le Corbusier, The Modulor; Fondation Le Corbusier.

q: Who designed the Farnsworth House?
n: Mies van der Rohe designed the Farnsworth House in Plano, Illinois (1945–51), a glass pavilion on a white steel frame raised above the floodplain. Source: Farnsworth House (National Trust) official site.

q: What style is the Farnsworth House?
n: The Farnsworth House is a pure International Style work: a steel frame, open plan, glass walls and no ornament. Organic modern is Wright's mode. Source: Farnsworth House official site; Encyclopaedia Britannica, International Style.

q: Which German-American architect, last director of the Bauhaus, led IIT's architecture department and shaped the Second Chicago School?
n: Mies van der Rohe was the last director of the Bauhaus (1930–33), then led the architecture department at IIT in Chicago from 1938. He was the central figure of the Second Chicago School. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe; IIT.

q: Who designed the German (Barcelona) Pavilion?
n: Mies van der Rohe designed the German Pavilion (Barcelona Pavilion) for the 1929 International Exposition in Barcelona, with Lilly Reich. Source: Fundació Mies van der Rohe.

q: When was the German Pavilion built?
n: The Barcelona Pavilion was built in 1929 for the International Exposition, dismantled in 1930 and rebuilt on site in 1983–86. Source: Fundació Mies van der Rohe.

q: Which Wright building is known for its strong horizontal lines?
n: The Robie House (Chicago, 1910) is the masterpiece of Wright's Prairie Style, with long low roofs, Roman brick and strong horizontal lines echoing the prairie. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust; UNESCO (20th-century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright).

q: Who designed the Robie House?
n: Frank Lloyd Wright designed the Frederick C. Robie House in Hyde Park, Chicago (1909–10). Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust; UNESCO.

q: Where is Casa Milà's most notable feature?
n: Casa Milà's most famous feature is its roof terrace, with sculptural chimneys, stair towers and ventilation shafts (the "warrior" chimneys). Source: La Pedrera official site; UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).

q: The large stone blocks used as statue materials in Casa Mila were quarried from:
n: Casa Milà's facade is built of limestone blocks from the Garraf and Vilafranca del Penedès quarries, cut and dressed into its undulating shape. That stone gave the building its nickname La Pedrera ("the quarry"). Source: La Pedrera official site (Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera).

q: Who designed the Gherkin in London?
n: 30 St Mary Axe ("the Gherkin," 2003) in the City of London was designed by Foster + Partners, with Arup as structural engineer. Source: Foster + Partners project page.

q: What is the primary function of the Gherkin building in London?
n: 30 St Mary Axe was built as the headquarters of Swiss Re and is a commercial office tower. Source: Foster + Partners project page; 30 St Mary Axe official site.

q: 30 St Mary Axe is informally called the:
n: 30 St Mary Axe is popularly called "the Gherkin" for its curved, pickle-like profile. Source: Foster + Partners; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What does Le Corbusier's béton brut mean?
n: Béton brut is French for "raw concrete," concrete left exposed with the imprint of its board formwork, as at Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation. It gave Brutalism its name. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Brutalism; Banham, The New Brutalism.

q: Which of these did Le Corbusier design?
n: Le Corbusier designed the Villa Savoye. The Glass House is Philip Johnson's, Fallingwater Frank Lloyd Wright's and the Barcelona Pavilion Mies van der Rohe's. Source: Fondation Le Corbusier; UNESCO.

q: What Barcelona building is known for its colorful, organic façade?
n: Casa Batlló (Passeig de Gràcia, Barcelona) is known for its colourful trencadís facade, bone-like columns and scaled, dragon-back roof. Source: Casa Batlló official site; UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí).

q: Who remodeled Casa Batlló, and when?
n: Antoni Gaudí remodelled Casa Batlló for Josep Batlló in 1904–1906. Source: Casa Batlló official site; UNESCO.

q: What is the English translation of the name Casa Batll6?
n: Casa Batlló is popularly called the "Casa dels Ossos" (House of Bones) for the skeletal, bone-like columns and balconies of its facade. Source: Casa Batlló official site.

q: Which style is Casa Batlló most associated with?
n: Casa Batlló is a key work of Catalan Modernisme, the Catalan form of Art Nouveau. Source: UNESCO (Works of Antoni Gaudí); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Art Nouveau.

q: What dominates Casa Batlló's façade?
n: Casa Batlló's facade is dominated by flowing, organic forms from nature: wave-like stone, bone-shaped columns, mask-like balconies and a scaled roof. There is no straight-line grid. Source: Casa Batlló official site.

q: In what year was Fallingwater completed?
n: Fallingwater was built in 1936–1939. The main house was occupied in 1937 and the guest wing finished in 1939. Source: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy (Fallingwater).

q: What is Fallingwater's most distinctive structural feature?
n: Fallingwater's defining structural feature is its reinforced-concrete cantilevered terraces projecting over the Bear Run waterfall, anchored to the rock core. Source: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What do Fallingwater's cantilevered slabs serve as?
n: Fallingwater's cantilevered slabs serve as outdoor terraces extending the living spaces over the stream. Source: Western Pennsylvania Conservancy.
